title: Stored Procedure Parameters, Handlers and Security
description: Create clear CALL contracts with IN and OUT parameters, then reason about transaction-owning handlers, driver results, and invoker versus definer security.

questions.question_text: How is a stored procedure invoked in the shown MySQL examples?
questions.explanation: CALL invokes the named procedure and its defined parameter contract.

questions.question_text: What does an IN parameter supply?
options: A table name chosen without validation
questions.explanation: Input values still need domain validation and authorized scope.

questions.question_text: What does an OUT parameter provide?
options: A returned value through the supported caller mechanism
questions.explanation: Driver handling differs from a normal result-set column.

questions.question_text: What is INOUT intended to do?
options: Accept a value and return its updated value
questions.explanation: Its input and output roles share the parameter.

questions.question_text: Does stored location alone prevent SQL injection?
options: Yes, all routine text is safe
Only if the routine has a short name
questions.explanation: Concatenated dynamic SQL can still treat input as structure.

questions.question_text: Why use p_region rather than an ambiguous region parameter name?
options: To make parameter and column ownership clear
questions.explanation: Clear scope prevents an accidental unfiltered comparison.

questions.question_text: What does the example NULL region comparison do?
options: It supplies no ordinary equality match
questions.explanation: Any all-regions policy must be explicitly implemented and authorized.

questions.question_text: What does ungrouped COUNT return for no matching approved rows?
questions.explanation: COUNT supplies its aggregate row with zero.

questions.question_text: Is DELIMITER a server SQL statement?
options: No, it is a client directive in supporting clients
questions.explanation: Creation tooling must distinguish client parsing from server syntax.

questions.question_text: Can a procedure’s COMMIT unexpectedly end caller-owned work?
options: No, every procedure has an independent transaction
questions.explanation: Transaction ownership must be agreed across callers and helpers.

questions.question_text: Does SQLEXCEPTION handling catch every zero-row business failure automatically?
options: Yes, zero rows always raise an exception
questions.explanation: Required effects can fail without a SQL error and need explicit checks.

questions.question_text: What can an EXIT handler with rollback affect in caller-owned work?
options: The caller’s earlier pending transaction effects
questions.explanation: A full rollback is not confined to an imagined nested child.

questions.question_text: What does SQL SECURITY INVOKER identify?
questions.explanation: Execution context and row authorization still require testing.

questions.question_text: Why is definer context sensitive?
options: It can expose privileges different from the caller’s
questions.explanation: The routine becomes a trusted capability boundary.

questions.question_text: Does an owner identifier supplied by a client prove ownership?
questions.explanation: Trusted identity and authorization must establish access.

questions.question_text: What should callers inspect when a routine contract changes?
options: Parameters, result shapes, ordering and errors
questions.explanation: Shared callers depend on observable behavior.

questions.question_text: Does a lost commit response prove the procedure rolled back?
questions.explanation: The server may have completed while the client lost confirmation.

questions.question_text: Does a procedure make external email reversible by SQL rollback?
options: Yes, if it is called inside BEGIN
questions.explanation: External effects need an explicit coordination design.

questions.question_text: What should the approved East fixture return when it has two approved and one cancelled order?
options: No rows because status is text
questions.explanation: The parameter and approval filter jointly define eligibility.

questions.question_text: What does a successful administrator fixture call fail to prove?
questions.explanation: Authorization needs allowed and denied tests at the actual context boundary.

coding_problems.title: Create a parameterized approved-order procedure
coding_problems.task: Create approved_region_orders(IN p_region VARCHAR(20)) with SQL SECURITY INVOKER. Return order_id and amount for approved rows in the requested region, ordered by order_id. Call the procedure for East.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE routine_orders(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,region VARCHAR(20),amount INT NOT NULL,status VARCHAR(12));
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE PROCEDURE approved_region_orders(IN p_region VARCHAR(20)) SQL SECURITY INVOKER SELECT order_id,amount FROM routine_orders WHERE region=p_region AND status='approved' ORDER BY order_id; CALL approved_region_orders('East');
coding_problems.ordering: Order by order_id inside the result-producing SELECT.
hints: Qualify the input population with both conditions.
coding_problems.explanation: The procedure applies the requested region and approved status before returning ordered detail.

coding_problems.title: Return an approved count through an OUT parameter
coding_problems.task: Create count_approved_orders(IN p_region VARCHAR(20), OUT p_count INT) with SQL SECURITY INVOKER. Set p_count to the approved row count for that region. Call it for East and return @approved_count AS approved_count.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE routine_orders(order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,region VARCHAR(20),amount INT NOT NULL,status VARCHAR(12));
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE PROCEDURE count_approved_orders(IN p_region VARCHAR(20),OUT p_count INT) SQL SECURITY INVOKER SELECT COUNT(*) INTO p_count FROM routine_orders WHERE region=p_region AND status='approved'; CALL count_approved_orders('East',@approved_count); SELECT @approved_count AS approved_count;
coding_problems.explanation: COUNT returns one known aggregate value even when no approved rows qualify.

notes:
## Package a database operation behind a defined call

A stored procedure is a named database program invoked with CALL. It can accept parameters, perform supported statements and return result sets or output values. It is useful when a shared database operation benefits from one reviewed contract close to the data. Storing logic in the database does not automatically make that logic secure, transactional or faster. Its inputs, privileges, side effects and completion ownership still need explicit design.

Imagine several reporting clients requesting approved workshop orders for one region. A procedure can define the eligible population and result columns once. A more sensitive procedure might reserve capacity, requiring trusted authorization and coordinated state checks. These operations have different privileges and failure requirements. Start with the caller-visible contract rather than creating one broad routine that accepts arbitrary SQL text or unrestricted table names.

## Distinguish procedure parameters and result channels

IN parameters provide input values. OUT parameters return values through the supported caller mechanism. INOUT parameters begin with a caller-supplied value and return its updated value. A SELECT without INTO can emit a result set from a procedure. Drivers need to handle the actual output contract, including multiple result sets or protocol status information, not assume every CALL behaves exactly like one ordinary SELECT.

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE approved_region_orders(IN p_region VARCHAR(20))
SQL SECURITY INVOKER
SELECT order_id,amount
FROM routine_orders
WHERE region=p_region AND status='approved'
ORDER BY order_id;
CALL approved_region_orders('East');
```

For East orders 1 approved 10, 2 cancelled 20 and 3 approved 30, the result contains 1/10 and 3/30. An unrelated West order is excluded. A NULL region parameter does not match NULL source regions under ordinary equality; that is the example's explicit comparison policy. If missing region means all regions, the procedure must implement and authorize that broader behavior deliberately rather than acquire it through an accidental OR condition.

## Keep parameter names distinct from column names

Use a naming convention such as p_region for parameters and qualify columns when scopes can be confused. A condition written region=region can become a tautology or bind names differently than intended. A report can then return every region while appearing correct on a fixture containing only East. Include at least two regions and different approval statuses to expose an omitted or misbound filter.

Parameters are values, not permission to choose arbitrary SQL structure. A prepared dynamic statement must still bind untrusted values and allow-list any structural variation. A stored routine that concatenates input into SQL can remain vulnerable to injection. SQL location is not the security boundary by itself; the final execution template and authorized resource scope must be reviewed.

## Use output values for an explicit aggregate contract

An OUT parameter can return one aggregate measure without emitting its underlying rows. For example, a count procedure can place the number of approved orders into p_count. COUNT returns zero for no matching orders, which differs from an ungrouped SUM returning NULL. Choose and document missing or empty behavior rather than expecting every aggregate to supply the same fallback.

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE count_approved_orders(
  IN p_region VARCHAR(20),OUT p_count INT
)
SQL SECURITY INVOKER
SELECT COUNT(*) INTO p_count
FROM routine_orders
WHERE region=p_region AND status='approved';
CALL count_approved_orders('East',@approved_count);
SELECT @approved_count AS approved_count;
```

The session variable is a client-visible mechanism for this SQL demonstration. An application driver can expose OUT values differently. Do not put private data in session variables and then return the connection to unrelated work without understanding its cleanup policy. Test the installed driver and connection pool rather than claiming the same parameter-binding interface across every client library.

## Define compound bodies and delimiter handling

A procedure containing several statements uses a compound BEGIN/END body with declarations and control flow where supported. Command-line clients often need a temporary DELIMITER setting so semicolons inside the body are not treated as the end of CREATE PROCEDURE. DELIMITER is a client directive, not a SQL statement the server executes. API migration tools and drivers can have different handling.

Declarations must follow the engine's placement and ordering rules. Keep local variable names and handler scopes easy to inspect. A demonstration that only works because a particular editor secretly changes delimiters is not a portable executable example. Record the client context for compound routine creation, and avoid inserting client-only commands into a driver API that expects one complete server statement.

## Assign transaction ownership before writing handlers

A procedure can participate in its caller's transaction. It must not silently issue COMMIT when the caller expects several operations to succeed together. Conversely, a routine explicitly designed to own a complete transaction needs an error path that resolves its unsuccessful work. MySQL does not create general independently nested transactions merely because a procedure calls another procedure.

A common transaction-owning pattern declares an EXIT handler for an appropriate error class, performs ROLLBACK and RESIGNAL, and commits only on the validated success path. That pattern is not automatically correct when embedded inside a caller-owned transaction, because rollback can discard the caller's earlier pending work. Define the owner and nesting contract first, then test the exact handler and engine error scopes.

## Separate statement errors from the business outcome

An UPDATE can affect no row without raising an SQL exception. A generic SQLEXCEPTION handler therefore does not prove that a required reservation or transfer occurred. The routine must check required effects and signal a failed business condition deliberately. A CHECK error can undo only its statement while earlier successful statements remain pending; an InnoDB deadlock can instead end the transaction. Error handling must respect those differences.

A network failure after CALL or COMMIT can also leave the client uncertain whether the server completed an operation. A stable authorized request identity and reconciliation path can prevent a retry from duplicating a completed effect. No stored-program label makes remote uncertainty disappear. Keep confirmed failure, confirmed success and unknown outcome distinct in the caller contract.

## Review invoker and definer security explicitly

SQL SECURITY INVOKER executes under the invoker context for the relevant privilege model. SQL SECURITY DEFINER uses the routine's definer context and can expose capabilities different from the caller's. MySQL routines default to definer security unless specified otherwise. A definer-context procedure is therefore a sensitive trusted operation, not a shortcut around authorization review.

Least privilege requires constraining which actions the routine exposes and which rows the caller may affect. An unrestricted owner parameter is not proof that the caller owns that resource. Test actual allowed and denied operations under the effective execution context in an isolated authorization environment. A read-only fixture called as an administrator does not establish production permission behavior, and this lesson does not modify any live grants.

## Keep interfaces stable and measure real costs

Callers can depend on parameter positions, types, result column names, ordering and error behavior. Changing a result set's shape can break mobile, web and reporting consumers even if the routine name remains unchanged. Inspect direct callers before evolving a shared routine. Version or coordinate a breaking contract rather than assuming database-local code has no application compatibility surface.

Stored logic can reduce round trips for some workflows, but per-row calls, poor plans or long transactions can still be expensive. Compare representative data and actual execution paths. Keep slow external work outside the protected transaction interval unless a reviewed protocol requires otherwise. Procedures do not make emails, files or remote payments participate in ordinary SQL rollback.

## Solve two routine-contract exercises

First exercise: create and call the approved-region procedure. Predict East's two eligible rows, then test a region containing only cancelled orders and a region with no rows. Both produce an empty result set under this contract. Include an unrelated low-numbered order to prove the parameter filter is active rather than merely an ordering coincidence.

Second exercise: create the OUT-count procedure and return the approved count for East. The expected value is two; an empty matching population returns zero. Explain why result-set output and an OUT parameter are different channels, and why neither establishes denied-access enforcement by itself. Continue with [transaction boundaries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transaction-boundaries), [database security](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/database-security-boundaries) and [nested transaction concepts](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/nested-transaction-concepts) for the trusted boundary surrounding a routine call.

diagrams.caption: A routine call has several separate contracts
diagrams.description: Input values define the requested scope, results define caller output, transaction ownership defines completion, and the security context defines privileges. None automatically supplies the other contracts.
rows: Caller or routine owns the transaction
